newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN SUGAR PRODUCERS CRITICISE THAI AID.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN SUGAR PRODUCERS CRITICISE THAI AID.

text.p: Australia's proposed A$1.3 billion contribution to a rescue package for Thailand may prove detrimental to the Australian sugar industry, Harry Bonanno, chairman of sugarcane grower organisation CANEGROWERS, said.
Thailand is Australia's major sugar export competitor in the Southeast Asian region and enjoys several inherent advantages, Bananno said in a statement on Tuesday.

Australia's sugarcane industry would be greatly alarmed if any of the Australian aid found its way into Thai sugar industry infrastructure, Bonanno said. "This would seriously jeopardise the future of the Australian sugar industry," he said.

Australia's industry was now totally exposed to unpredictable world market prices and even before the recent removal of Australia's tariff on sugar imports had the lowest domestic support level of any sugar exporting country, he said.
"We have enough disadvantages without creating new ones," Bonanno said.

He said it was ironic that the Australian government seemed to have no difficulty finding a massive amount of money to bail out the Thai economy when it found it so hard to provide funding to compensate its own cane growers for the recent loss of the sugar import tariff, he said.
Drought-stricken cane growers in the Bundaberg region of Queensland were in "desperate straits" because of inadequate funding of water infrastructure, he said.
They would look with a very jaundiced eye at "mega-dollar aid" to Australia's leading sugar export competitor, he said.
Like Australia, Thailand exported most of its sugar to the world market, he said.
Unlike Australia, he said, it did so with strong government support and substantial cross-subsidies from the 25 percent of sugar it sold to its domestic market at highly inflated prices.

Thailand was already a low-cost sugar producer and had shown itself to be highly responsive to market opportunities, Bonanno said. Thailand already grew more sugarcane than Australia and had been undergoing a positive transformation. It also faced lower wage costs than the Australian industry, he added.
Australia's federal government has announced it will contribute up to A$1.35 billion to a US$15 billion International Monetary Fund rescue package for Thailand through a currency swap.
